1.question: What does HTML stand for?
1.explanation: HTML stands for Hyper Text Markup Language and is used to structure web pages.

1.question: Which DOCTYPE declaration is used for modern HTML5 documents?
1.explanation: <!DOCTYPE html> is the standard and simple DOCTYPE declaration in HTML5.

1.question: What is the root element of an HTML document?
1.explanation: The <html> element is the root element of an HTML page, wrapping all other elements.

1.question: Which element contains metadata and links to scripts and stylesheets?
1.explanation: The <head> element contains machine-readable information (metadata) like title, styles, and scripts.

1.question: Which HTML element contains the visible content of a web page?
1.explanation: The <body> element defines the document's body and contains all the visible content.

1.question: Which tag is used to set the document title shown on the browser tab?
1.explanation: The <title> tag inside <head> defines the title of the document shown in the browser tab.

1.question: Which HTML tag represents the highest level and largest default heading?
1.explanation: <h1> represents the highest level heading and is the largest by default.

1.question: Which tag represents the smallest and lowest level standard heading in HTML?
1.explanation: <h6> defines the smallest and least significant standard HTML heading.

1.question: Which HTML element is used to define a regular paragraph of text?
1.explanation:
The

element is used to define paragraphs in HTML.

1.question: What is the correct HTML element for inserting a single line break?
1.explanation: inserts a single line break without creating a new paragraph.

1.question: Which HTML tag is used to insert a horizontal line or thematic break?
1.explanation: <hr> produces a horizontal rule / thematic break between paragraph-level elements.

1.question: What is the correct syntax for writing a comment in HTML?
1.explanation: HTML comments start with <!-- and end with -->.

1.question: Which file extension is standard for saving HTML files?
1.explanation: HTML files are saved with either .html or .htm extensions.

1.question: Is HTML case-sensitive for standard element names?
options: No, HTML tag names are case-insensitive
1.explanation: HTML tag names are not case-sensitive, though lowercase is recommended by W3C.

1.question:
What kind of element is
in HTML?
1.explanation:
The
tag is an empty/void element because it does not have a closing tag or inner content.

1.question: Which tag is used to render text in bold without conveying extra semantic importance?
1.explanation: <b> makes text bold purely for stylistic presentation.

1.question: Which HTML tag is used to render text in bold while conveying strong semantic importance?
1.explanation: <strong> conveys that the text has strong importance, seriousness, or urgency, rendered bold by default.

1.question: Which tag is used to display italic text without conveying extra semantic emphasis?
1.explanation: The <i> tag renders text in italic for styling or alternative voice.

1.question: Which HTML tag provides semantic emphasis that alters the tone of text when read by a screen reader?
1.explanation: The <em> element is used for stress emphasis, read with different inflection by screen readers.

1.question: Which HTML tag is used to render underlined text?
1.explanation: The <u> tag represents text that is unarticulated or underlined.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used to create subscript text, such as in chemical formulas like H2O?
2.explanation: <sub> defines subscript text, appearing half a character below the normal baseline.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used to create superscript text, such as in exponents like x2?
2.explanation: <sup> defines superscript text, appearing half a character above the normal baseline.

2.question: Which tag is used to highlight or mark text with a yellow background by default?
2.explanation: The <mark> element represents text marked or highlighted for reference purposes.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used to display deleted/struck-through text?
2.explanation: The <del> element represents text that has been deleted from a document.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used to represent inserted or newly added text with an underline by default?
2.explanation: The <ins> element represents text that has been inserted into a document.

2.question: Which tag is used to render small print, such as copyright and legal notices?
2.explanation: The <small> element renders side-comments and small print like legal disclaimers.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used for long quotations indented from the surrounding text?
2.explanation: <blockquote> is used for section quotes that are usually displayed with left/right indentation.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used for short, inline quotations with automatic quotation marks?
2.explanation: The <q> element defines a short inline quotation where browsers automatically insert quotation marks.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used to define the title or reference of a creative work?
2.explanation: The <cite> tag defines the title of a creative work like a book, song, or movie.

2.question: Which tag is used to display preformatted text preserving exact spaces and line breaks?
2.explanation: The <pre> element displays text in a fixed-width font preserving whitespace and line breaks.

2.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a hyperlink?
2.explanation: The <a> (anchor) tag is used to define hyperlinks to other web pages or locations.

2.question: Which attribute is required on an anchor tag to specify the destination URL?
2.explanation: The href (Hypertext REFerence) attribute specifies the URL destination of the link.

2.question: Which target attribute value opens a link in a new browser tab or window?
2.explanation: target='_blank' causes the linked document to open in a new tab or window.

2.question: What is the default value of the target attribute for an HTML link?
2.explanation: _self is the default value, opening the link in the same window/frame.

2.question: Which prefix is used in the href attribute to create an email link?
2.explanation: mailto: followed by an email address opens the user's default email client.

2.question: Which prefix is used in the href attribute to create a clickable telephone link?
2.explanation: tel: allows mobile devices to dial the phone number directly when clicked.

2.question: How do you link to a specific section on the same page with id='contact'?
2.explanation: Using a hash symbol with the id (href='#contact') links directly to that page fragment.

2.question: What is a relative URL in HTML?
options: A link that points to a specific file relative to the current folder or domain
A link that only opens on localhost
A link with a full https:// address
2.explanation: A relative URL points to a file relative to the current document rather than an absolute web address.

2.question: What is an absolute URL in HTML?
options: A complete URL including protocol and domain name
A link with an anchor tag #
A URL with only a filename
2.explanation: An absolute URL contains the complete address including the protocol (e.g., https://example.com/page.html).

2.question: Which attribute specifies the relationship between the current document and the linked document?
2.explanation: The rel attribute defines the relationship, such as rel='noopener noreferrer' or rel='stylesheet'.

3.question: Why is rel='noopener' recommended when using target='_blank'?
options: It prevents security vulnerabilities by disallowing window.opener access
It caches the page in local storage
3.explanation: rel='noopener' prevents the opened page from accessing the window.opener object of the original page.

3.question: Which element is used to link an external CSS stylesheet inside the <head> tag?
3.explanation: <link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'> links external stylesheets.

3.question: Can an anchor tag wrap an image element to make the image clickable?
options: No, anchor tags only accept text
Only if the image is in SVG format
3.explanation: Wrapping an tag with an tag turns the image into a clickable hyperlink.

3.question: Which attribute can provide a tooltip when a user hovers over a link?
3.explanation: The title attribute displays a small tooltip containing the text when hovered.

3.question: How can you link to the top of the current web page?
3.explanation: href='#' or href='#top' scrolls the browser back to the top of the current page.

3.question: Which tag is used to embed an image in an HTML document?
3.explanation: The element is used to embed images on a web page.

3.question: Which attribute is used to specify the file path or URL of an image?
3.explanation: The src (source) attribute specifies the URL or path of the image to display.

3.question: What does the alt attribute in an tag do?
options: Provides alternative text if the image fails to load and for accessibility screen readers
3.explanation: The alt attribute provides descriptive text for screen readers and displays when the image fails to load.

3.question: Which attributes are used to define the width and height of an image in HTML?
3.explanation: width and height attributes define dimensions in pixels directly on the tag.

3.question: Is the tag an empty (self-closing) element?
options: Yes, it has no closing tag in HTML5
3.explanation: is a void element and does not have a closing tag.

3.question: Which tag is used to wrap an image and its associated caption together semantically?
3.explanation: The <figure> element encapsulates media like illustrations, photos, or diagrams.

3.question: Which tag is used to provide a caption for a <figure> element?
3.explanation: <figcaption> provides a caption or legend inside a <figure> element.

3.question: Which HTML5 element is used to embed audio files like MP3s natively?
3.explanation: The <audio> element is used to play audio files natively on a web page.

3.question: Which attribute must be added to <audio> or <video> to show default play/pause buttons?
3.explanation: The controls attribute displays the native audio/video playback interface.

3.question: Which HTML5 element is used to embed video files natively?
3.explanation: The <video> element embeds video streams directly in the browser without plugins.

3.question: Which child tag is used inside <audio> or <video> to specify multiple media source formats?
3.explanation: <source> tags specify alternative video/audio files so the browser can choose the supported format.

3.question: Which HTML tag is used to embed an external web page inside the current document?
3.explanation: The <iframe> (inline frame) element embeds another HTML page within the current document.

3.question: Which HTML5 element provides a drawing surface for 2D/3D graphics via JavaScript?
3.explanation: The <canvas> tag provides an API for rendering dynamic, scriptable 2D/3D shapes and bitmaps.

3.question: Which HTML tag is used to create an ordered (numbered) list?
3.explanation: <ol> defines an ordered list where list items are numbered by default.

3.question: Which HTML tag is used to create an unordered (bulleted) list?
3.explanation: <ul> defines an unordered list where list items are marked with bullets.

4.question: Which tag defines an individual list item in both ordered and unordered lists?
4.explanation: <li> (List Item) is used inside <ol> and <ul> to define individual items.

4.question: Which tag is used to create a description or definition list?
4.explanation: <dl> (Description List) contains term-definition groups.

4.question: Which tag specifies the term/name in a description list?
4.explanation: <dt> defines a term/name in a description list (<dl>).

4.question: Which tag specifies the description or definition of a term in a description list?
4.explanation: <dd> defines the description/value for the preceding <dt>.

4.question: Which attribute can change the numbering style of an ordered list in HTML?
4.explanation: The type attribute ('1', 'a', 'A', 'i', 'I') sets the numbering scheme for an <ol>.

4.question: Which attribute allows an ordered list to start from a specific number like 5?
4.explanation: start='5' configures the starting number of an ordered list.

4.question: Which boolean attribute reverses the numbering order of an <ol> in HTML5?
4.explanation: The reversed attribute numbers list items in descending order.

4.question: Can a list be placed inside another list item to create a nested list?
options: Yes, lists can be nested inside <li> elements
4.explanation: Nesting lists inside <li> elements is standard for creating submenus and multi-level hierarchies.

4.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a table?
4.explanation: The <table> tag creates a tabular data grid in HTML.

4.question: Which tag defines a table row?
4.explanation: <tr> stands for Table Row and defines a horizontal row of cells.

4.question: Which tag defines a standard table data cell?
4.explanation: <td> stands for Table Data and defines a standard content cell.

4.question: Which tag defines a header cell in a table, rendered bold and centered by default?
4.explanation: <th> stands for Table Header and renders header cells prominently.

4.question: Which tag provides a title or caption for an entire table?
4.explanation: The <caption> element provides an accessible title displayed above the table.

4.question: Which attribute is used to make a table cell span across multiple columns horizontally?
4.explanation: colspan='2' merges a cell across 2 columns horizontally.

4.question: Which attribute is used to make a table cell span across multiple rows vertically?
4.explanation: rowspan='2' merges a cell across 2 rows vertically.

4.question: Which semantic tag groups the header rows in a table?
4.explanation: <thead> groups header content within an HTML table.

4.question: Which semantic tag groups the body data rows in a table?
4.explanation: <tbody> groups the main body data rows in an HTML table.

4.question: Which semantic tag groups the summary or footer rows in a table?
4.explanation: <tfoot> groups footer summary rows in an HTML table.

4.question: What does the scope attribute in a <th> element do?
options: Identifies whether the header is for a row, col, rowgroup, or colgroup
4.explanation: The scope attribute ('row' or 'col') clarifies table structure for screen readers.

4.question: Which HTML element is used to create an interactive user input form?
4.explanation: The <form> element wraps controls for submitting data to a server.

5.question: Which attribute in a <form> specifies where to send the form data on submit?
5.explanation: The action attribute specifies the URL/endpoint to which form data is sent.

5.question: Which attribute defines the HTTP method used when submitting a form?
5.explanation: The method attribute specifies 'GET' or 'POST' HTTP methods for submission.

5.question: Which input type is used for single-line plain text entry?
5.explanation: <input type='text'> creates a single-line text input field.

5.question: Which input type hides characters as bullets for secret input?
5.explanation: <input type='password'> masks entered characters for security.

5.question: Which input type creates a clickable toggle for selecting multiple independent options?
5.explanation: <input type='checkbox'> allows users to select zero, one, or multiple items.

5.question: Which input type allows selecting only one option from a mutually exclusive group?
5.explanation: <input type='radio'> with matching name attributes ensures only one option is chosen.

5.question: Which element is used to associate a descriptive text label with an input field?
5.explanation: The <label> tag associates descriptive text with a form input via the 'for' attribute.

5.question: Which attribute connects a <label> to an <input> element's id?
5.explanation: The for attribute of a <label> matches the id of the target input.

5.question: Which element is used to create a multi-line text input area?
5.explanation: The <textarea> tag creates a resizable, multi-line text input area.

5.question: Which element creates a drop-down selection menu?
5.explanation: The <select> element creates a drop-down list of choices.

5.question: Which tag defines an individual selectable item inside a <select> dropdown?
5.explanation: The <option> tag defines options within a <select> element.

5.question: Which attribute in an input field displays ghost placeholder text before user typing?
5.explanation: The placeholder attribute displays a helpful hint inside the input box.

5.question: Which HTML5 element represents the primary content area unique to the document?
5.explanation: The <main> tag represents the dominant content of the document body.

5.question: Which semantic element represents introductory content, logos, or navigation aids?
5.explanation: The <header> element contains introductory content or site navigation.

5.question: Which semantic element is specifically intended for site navigation links?
5.explanation: The <nav> element designates major navigation link sections.

5.question: Which element represents a self-contained, independently distributable composition like a blog post?
5.explanation: The <article> element represents a standalone, reusable piece of content.

5.question: Which element represents content tangentially related to the main content, such as a sidebar?
5.explanation: The <aside> element defines secondary or sidebar content.

5.question: What is the primary difference between a <div> and a <span> in HTML?
options: <div> is a block-level container; <span> is an inline container
5.explanation: <div> is a generic block-level container, whereas <span> is an inline container.

5.question: Which attribute is used to give an HTML element a globally unique identifier?
5.explanation: The id attribute provides a unique identifier for an element on the page.

5.question: Which attribute specifies the human language of the HTML document content (e.g. lang='en')?
5.explanation: The lang attribute on <html> specifies the primary natural language of the page content.

1.question: What does CSS stand for?
1.explanation: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets, used to format the layout of web pages.

1.question:
What is the correct CSS syntax to select all

elements and color them red?
1.explanation: In CSS, element selectors use the tag name followed by curly braces: p { color: red; }.

1.question: In the CSS rule 'h1 { color: blue; }', what is 'color' called?
1.explanation: 'color' is the property name, while 'blue' is its assigned value.

1.question: In the CSS rule 'p { font-size: 16px; }', what is '16px' called?
1.explanation: '16px' is the value assigned to the property 'font-size'.

1.question: Which character is used to separate CSS property names from their values?
1.explanation: A colon (:) separates the property name from its value in a CSS declaration.

1.question: Which character is used to end each CSS declaration statement?
1.explanation: A semicolon (;) terminates each individual CSS declaration within a rule.

1.question: Which symbol is used to define comments in CSS?
1.explanation: CSS comments start with /* and end with */.

1.question: Which HTML element is used to define internal CSS within the <head> section?
1.explanation: The <style> tag defines internal CSS rules within the <head> of an HTML document.

1.question: Which HTML tag is used to reference an external CSS stylesheet file?
1.explanation: The <link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'> tag is used to attach external CSS files.

1.question: Which HTML attribute is used to apply inline CSS styles directly to an element?
1.explanation: The style attribute allows inline CSS declarations directly inside an HTML tag.

1.question: Which CSS method is considered best practice for large multi-page websites?
options: Internal style tags on each page
1.explanation: External stylesheets allow site-wide style reuse and easy centralized maintenance.

1.question: What does the 'Cascading' in CSS mean?
options: Styles are generated automatically by servers
Rules flow top-to-bottom and inherit styles based on specificity and source order
CSS only works with waterfall layouts
Styles cannot be overridden once defined
1.explanation: Cascading refers to the hierarchy and precedence algorithm that decides which style rules apply.

1.question: Which character is used to write an ID selector in CSS?
1.explanation: The hash symbol (#) selects elements by their unique id attribute (e.g., #header).

1.question: Which character is used to write a class selector in CSS?
1.explanation: The period (.) character targets elements with that class name (e.g., .btn).

1.question: Which selector selects ALL elements on a web page?
1.explanation: The asterisk (*) represents the universal selector, targeting every element in the DOM.

1.question: How do you group multiple selectors in CSS to share the same rule?
options: Separate selectors with commas (h1, h2, p)
Separate selectors with plus signs (h1 + h2)
1.explanation: Commas allow grouping selectors so they share a declaration block: h1, h2, p { ... }.

1.question: What is a descendant selector in CSS?
options:
div p (Selects any

inside a

at any depth)
1.explanation:
A space between selectors (div p) targets any

element nested anywhere inside a

.

1.question: Which selector targets direct child elements only?
1.explanation: The child combinator (>) selects elements that are immediate direct children of the parent.

1.question: Which selector targets an input element with type='text'?
1.explanation: Attribute selectors use square brackets: input[type='text'].

1.question: What is the CSS specificity priority from highest to lowest?
1.explanation: Inline styles have the highest priority, followed by ID selectors, then Class/attribute selectors, then Element selectors.

2.question: Which keyword forces a CSS rule to override other styles regardless of specificity?
2.explanation: !important gives a declaration top precedence in the cascade.

2.question: What does the selector '.card p' target?
options: All paragraphs that are descendants of elements with class 'card'
Only paragraphs that also have class 'card'
2.explanation:
It selects all

elements nested inside an element that has the class .card.

2.question: What does the compound selector 'p.intro' target?
options:
Only

elements that specifically have the class 'intro'
2.explanation:
Without spaces, p.intro selects

elements that have class='intro'.

2.question: Which pseudo-class targets an element when the user hovers over it with a cursor?
2.explanation: :hover matches when the user designates an element with a pointing device.

2.question: Which pseudo-class applies when an interactive element (like an input) receives keyboard focus?
2.explanation: :focus applies when an element gains focus, such as clicking into a text box.

2.question: Which pseudo-class applies while an element is being actively clicked / pressed?
2.explanation: :active applies during the active click/press action by the user.

2.question: Which pseudo-class targets an unvisited hyperlink?
2.explanation: :link targets links that have not yet been visited by the user.

2.question: Which pseudo-class targets hyperlinks that have already been visited?
2.explanation: :visited styles links that exist in the user's browser history.

2.question: Which CSS property changes the text color of an element?
2.explanation: The 'color' property sets the foreground color of text content.

2.question: Which CSS property changes the background color of an element?
2.explanation: The 'background-color' property defines the background fill color of an element.

2.question: Which of the following is a valid 6-character Hex color code for pure white?
2.explanation: #FFFFFF (or #FFF) represents pure white in hexadecimal RGB.

2.question: In the RGB color model rgb(255, 0, 0), which color is displayed?
2.explanation: 255 on the red channel with 0 on green and blue gives pure red.

2.question: What does the 'A' stand for in rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)?
2.explanation: Alpha defines the opacity level between 0.0 (completely transparent) and 1.0 (completely opaque).

2.question: What does HSL stand for in CSS color definitions?
2.explanation: HSL represents colors via Hue (degrees 0-360), Saturation (%), and Lightness (%).

2.question: Which CSS property is used to set an image as a background?
2.explanation: background-image: url('image.jpg'); sets a background image.

2.question: Which property value prevents a background image from repeating across the container?
2.explanation: background-repeat: no-repeat; ensures the image displays only once.

2.question: Which property value scales a background image to completely cover the entire container?
2.explanation: background-size: cover; scales the image proportionally so the background area is completely covered.

2.question: Which property value scales a background image so that the entire image fits inside without cropping?
2.explanation: background-size: contain; scales the image to fit entirely within the container boundaries.

2.question: Which CSS property sets the transparency level of an entire element including its contents?
2.explanation: The opacity property (0.0 to 1.0) adjusts transparency for an element and its children.

2.question: Which CSS function creates a smooth transition between two or more colors as a background?
2.explanation: linear-gradient(direction, color1, color2) creates smooth gradient backgrounds.

3.question: Which CSS property sets the position of a background image inside its container?
3.explanation: background-position (e.g., center, top left) controls the placement of the background image.

3.question: Which keyword makes a background color completely invisible without hiding child elements?
3.explanation: background-color: transparent; produces a see-through background fill.

3.question: Which CSS property controls the size of text?
3.explanation: font-size (e.g. 16px, 1.2rem) specifies the height of font glyphs.

3.question: Which CSS property specifies the font typeface for an element?
3.explanation: font-family specifies a prioritized list of font names (e.g. 'Inter', sans-serif).

3.question: Which property is used to make text bold or light?
3.explanation: font-weight accepts values like bold, normal, 400, 600, 700.

3.question: Which CSS property aligns text horizontally to the left, center, or right?
3.explanation: text-align (left, center, right, justify) sets the horizontal alignment of inline contents.

3.question: Which property is used to remove default underlines from hyperlinks?
3.explanation: text-decoration: none; removes default underlines from <a> anchor tags.

3.question: Which CSS property controls the vertical spacing between lines of text?
3.explanation: line-height controls the distance between baselines of successive lines of text.

3.question: Which CSS property controls the horizontal spacing between characters?
3.explanation: letter-spacing adjusts the horizontal space between individual letters/characters.

3.question: Which CSS property changes text capitalization to UPPERCASE, lowercase, or Capitalize?
3.explanation: text-transform (uppercase, lowercase, capitalize) alters text case presentation.

3.question: Which property makes text italic in CSS?
3.explanation: font-style: italic; slants the typography into italics.

3.question: Which CSS unit is relative to the root <html> element's font size?
3.explanation: rem (Root EM) is relative to the font-size of the root <html> element (usually 16px).

3.question: Which CSS unit is relative to the font-size of its direct parent element?
3.explanation: em is relative to the font-size of the element's parent.

3.question: Which unit represents 1% of the viewport width?
3.explanation: vw stands for Viewport Width (100vw = 100% of browser window width).

3.question: Which unit represents 1% of the viewport height?
3.explanation: vh stands for Viewport Height (100vh = 100% of browser window height).

3.question: What are the 4 core components of the CSS Box Model from inside to outside?
3.explanation: From inside out: Content -> Padding -> Border -> Margin.

3.question: Which part of the Box Model creates space immediately around content inside the border?
3.explanation: Padding is the clear space between the content and the element's border.

3.question: Which part of the Box Model creates space outside the element's border, separating it from neighbors?
3.explanation: Margin clears an area outside the border, creating breathing room between adjacent elements.

3.question: In the shorthand 'margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;', which side has 20px margin?
3.explanation: Clockwise order: Top (10px), Right (20px), Bottom (30px), Left (40px).

3.question: In the 2-value shorthand 'padding: 10px 20px;', what does 20px represent?
3.explanation: With 2 values: the first value applies to Top/Bottom, and the second applies to Left/Right.

4.question: What does 'box-sizing: border-box;' do?
options: Includes padding and border within the element's specified width and height
4.explanation: border-box ensures that width/height include content, padding, and borders, preventing layout blowouts.

4.question: What is the default browser value of the 'box-sizing' property?
4.explanation: The default value is content-box, where padding and borders add onto specified dimensions.

4.question: How do you center a block element horizontally with a defined width?
4.explanation: margin: 0 auto; evenly distributes available horizontal margin, centering the element.

4.question: Which CSS property rounds the corners of an element's border?
4.explanation: border-radius (e.g., border-radius: 8px; or 50% for circles) rounds the corners.

4.question: Which property is required for a border to be visible?
4.explanation: border-style (e.g. solid, dashed) is mandatory; without it, borders have a default style of 'none'.

4.question: Which property creates a soft drop shadow behind an element's box?
4.explanation: box-shadow (e.g., box-shadow: 0 4px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.1);) creates outer or inner shadows.

4.question: What is the difference between margin and padding?
options: Margin is outside the border, padding is inside the border
Margin adds background color, padding is transparent
Margin is inside the border, padding is outside
4.explanation: Padding adds space inside the border; Margin creates space outside the border.

4.question: Can negative margin values be used to pull elements closer together in CSS?
options: No, CSS returns an error on negative margins
Yes, negative margins are valid in CSS
4.explanation: Negative margins (e.g., margin-top: -10px;) pull elements in the corresponding direction.

4.question: What is the default display property of a <div> element?
4.explanation: <div> elements are display: block by default, starting on a new line and taking full available width.

4.question: What is the default display property of a <span> element?
4.explanation: <span> elements are display: inline by default, only taking up as much width as necessary.

4.question: Which display value hides an element completely and removes it from the document layout flow?
4.explanation: display: none; removes the element entirely from the page layout flow.

4.question: What is the difference between 'display: none;' and 'visibility: hidden;'?
options: 'display: none' removes the element from layout flow; 'visibility: hidden' hides it while preserving its space
They are identical in all ways
'display: none' preserves space; 'visibility: hidden' does not
4.explanation: visibility: hidden makes the element invisible but keeps its empty space in the layout.

4.question: What is the default position property value of HTML elements?
4.explanation: static is the default positioning; elements flow naturally according to standard page order.

4.question: When an element is set to 'position: relative;', what is it positioned relative to?
options: Its normal static position in document flow
4.explanation: position: relative offsets the element from where it would normally have been placed without disrupting flow.

4.question: When an element is set to 'position: absolute;', what is it positioned relative to?
options: Its nearest ancestor with a position other than static
4.explanation: An absolute element positions itself relative to its closest non-static ancestor (or the initial containing block).

4.question: Which position value fixes an element relative to the browser viewport, keeping it visible on scroll?
4.explanation: position: fixed keeps the element pinned to the viewport even when the page is scrolled.

4.question: Which position value toggles between relative and fixed depending on the scroll position?
4.explanation: position: sticky behaves like relative until a scroll threshold is met, where it sticks like fixed.

4.question: Which CSS property controls the stacking order of overlapping positioned elements?
4.explanation: z-index controls 3D stacking order along the z-axis for positioned elements.

4.question: Which property controls how content that exceeds its container's boundaries is handled?
4.explanation: overflow (visible, hidden, scroll, auto) manages content that spills outside its box.

4.question: Which value of overflow adds scrollbars ONLY when the content actually overflows?
4.explanation: overflow: auto adds scrollbars only when the inner content exceeds the container dimensions.

5.question: Which declaration enables Flexbox on a container element?
5.explanation: display: flex turns a container into a flex container.

5.question: Which flex property changes the main axis direction to vertical columns?
5.explanation: flex-direction: column arranges flex items vertically from top to bottom.

5.question: Which property aligns flex items along the MAIN axis (horizontal by default)?
5.explanation: justify-content (flex-start, center, space-between, space-around) aligns items along the main axis.

5.question: Which property aligns flex items along the CROSS axis (perpendicular to main axis)?
5.explanation: align-items (flex-start, center, flex-end, stretch) aligns items along the cross axis.

5.question: Which Flexbox property allows flex items to wrap onto multiple lines if space is insufficient?
5.explanation: flex-wrap: wrap allows flex items to break onto multiple rows/columns.

5.question: Which property sets the spacing/gutters between flex or grid items?
5.explanation: The 'gap' property sets the space between rows and columns in flex and grid layouts.

5.question: Which shorthand flex item property combines grow, shrink, and basis?
5.explanation: flex: 1 (short for flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis) allows an item to expand evenly.

5.question: Which declaration enables CSS Grid layout on a container?
5.explanation: display: grid turns the element into a grid formatting context container.

5.question: Which CSS Grid property defines the number and widths of columns?
5.explanation: grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); defines 3 equal columns in CSS Grid.

5.question: What does the '1fr' unit represent in CSS Grid?
options: One fraction of the available free space in the grid container
5.explanation: 1fr represents one fraction of the remaining available space in the grid container.

5.question: Which pseudo-element is used to insert cosmetic content BEFORE an element's content via CSS?
5.explanation: ::before inserts a pseudo-element before the element's actual content (requires content: '').

5.question: Which CSS property must always be present in a ::before or ::after pseudo-element to render?
5.explanation: The 'content' property (e.g. content: '';) is mandatory for pseudo-elements to be created.

5.question: Which CSS property enables smooth animated changes between state property values?
5.explanation: The transition property (e.g. transition: all 0.3s ease;) animates property state transitions smoothly.

5.question: Which property is used to scale, rotate, translate, or skew an element in 2D/3D space?
5.explanation: transform (e.g. transform: scale(1.05); or rotate(45deg);) applies visual geometric changes.

5.question: Which CSS at-rule is used to apply different styles depending on screen size / device capabilities?
5.explanation: @media queries (e.g., @media (max-width: 768px)) apply conditional styles for responsive design.

5.question: What does '@media (max-width: 768px)' mean?
options: Styles apply only when the viewport width is 768px or narrower (tablets and mobile)
5.explanation: max-width: 768px targets screens from 0px up to 768px wide.

5.question: What is 'Mobile-First' design in responsive CSS?
options: Writing base styles for mobile devices first and scaling up with min-width media queries
Writing desktop styles first and overriding with max-width queries
Building separate apps for iOS and Android
5.explanation: Mobile-First begins with mobile base styles and adds min-width breakpoints for larger viewports.

5.question: Which CSS property changes the mouse cursor icon when hovering over an element?
5.explanation: cursor: pointer; changes the cursor to a clicking hand pointer.

5.question: Which property controls whether an element can respond to mouse/pointer click events?
5.explanation: pointer-events: none; makes an element pass all click events through to elements beneath it.

5.question: Which CSS property specifies how text selection behaves when a user highlights text?
5.explanation: user-select: none; prevents users from highlighting/selecting text on the element.

1.question: What is the difference between 'let' and 'var' in terms of scope in JavaScript?
1.explanation: 'let' and 'const' have block scope (enclosed by {}), whereas 'var' has function scope.

1.question: What happens if you try to reassign a variable declared with 'const' (e.g. const x = 10; x = 20;)?
options: It throws a TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
It creates a new global variable
1.explanation: Variables declared with 'const' cannot be reassigned after declaration.

1.question: Can you modify properties of an object declared with 'const' (e.g. const user = { name: 'Alex' }; user.name = 'Sam';)?
options: Yes, the object reference is constant, but its properties are mutable
No, const makes all properties immutable
1.explanation: 'const' prevents reassigning the variable identifier itself, but the mutated properties inside an object can still change.

1.question: What is the 'Temporal Dead Zone' (TDZ) in JavaScript?
options: The memory allocated for async functions
The time taken by setTimeout to execute
The period between entering scope and variable declaration with let/const where accessing it throws a ReferenceError
A zone where garbage collection runs
1.explanation: Accessing 'let' or 'const' variables before their declaration line results in a ReferenceError due to TDZ.

1.question: What will be logged by: console.log(typeof null);?
1.explanation: Due to a historical implementation quirk in JavaScript, typeof null evaluates to 'object'.

1.question: What is the output of: console.log(typeof NaN);?
1.explanation: NaN stands for Not-a-Number, but its official JavaScript data type is 'number'.

1.question: What will be the output of: console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);?
1.explanation: Due to IEEE 754 binary floating-point representation, 0.1 + 0.2 is approx 0.30000000000000004, so it does not strictly equal 0.3.

1.question: What is the result of evaluating: console.log('5' - 2);?
1.explanation: The subtraction operator (-) converts numeric strings to numbers, computing 5 - 2 = 3.

1.question: What is the result of evaluating: console.log('5' + 2);?
1.explanation: The addition operator (+) with a string operand performs string concatenation, resulting in '52'.

1.question: What is the output of: console.log(typeof undeclaredVar);?
1.explanation: Using typeof on an undeclared variable safely returns 'undefined' without throwing an error.

1.question: Which of the following is a primitive data type introduced in ES6?
1.explanation: Symbol was introduced in ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) as a unique, immutable primitive value.

1.question: What is the result of: console.log([] == false);?
1.explanation: Both operands undergo type coercion: [] becomes '' (empty string), which coerces to 0, and false coerces to 0 (0 == 0 is true).

1.question: What is the key difference between loose equality (==) and strict equality (===)?
options: == performs type coercion before comparison; === requires both same value and same type
== checks only data type; === checks only value
1.explanation: Strict equality (===) checks value and type without type conversion, whereas == coerces operands to matching types.

1.question: What will be logged by: console.log(null == undefined); and console.log(null === undefined);?
1.explanation: null == undefined is true (loose equality), but null === undefined is false (different types).

1.question: What does the nullish coalescing operator (??) do?
options: Returns the right-hand operand only if the left is null or undefined
Returns right-hand operand if left is any falsy value (including 0, '')
1.explanation: ?? only falls back when the left operand is strictly null or undefined, unlike || which checks all falsy values.

1.question: What will be the output of: const val = 0 ?? 10; console.log(val);?
1.explanation: Because 0 is neither null nor undefined, ?? preserves 0.

1.question: What will be the output of: const val = 0 || 10; console.log(val);?
1.explanation: Because 0 is falsy, || evaluates and returns the right-hand operand 10.

1.question: What does the optional chaining operator (?.) do in JavaScript?
options: Safely accesses nested object properties without throwing error if a reference is nullish
1.explanation: Optional chaining (user?.address?.city) short-circuits to undefined if user or address is null/undefined.

1.question: What will be the output of: console.log(true + false);?
1.explanation: Booleans coerce to numbers when using the arithmetic + operator: true becomes 1, false becomes 0, 1 + 0 = 1.

1.question: What will be the output of: console.log(Boolean('')); and console.log(Boolean('false'));?
1.explanation: Empty string '' is falsy (false), while any non-empty string like 'false' is truthy (true).

2.question: Which of the following values is NOT falsy in JavaScript?
2.explanation: Empty objects {} and empty arrays [] are truthy in JavaScript.

2.question: What is the output of: console.log(1 < 2 < 3); and console.log(3 > 2 > 1);?
2.explanation: 1 < 2 evaluates to true -> true < 3 -> 1 < 3 (true). But 3 > 2 is true -> true > 1 -> 1 > 1 (false).

2.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
options: A function that has no return statement
A method to close browser tabs
A function that retains access to its outer (lexical) scope variables even after the outer function has executed
2.explanation: A closure gives an inner function access to its outer enclosing function's variables.

2.question: What is the primary difference in 'this' binding between arrow functions and regular function declarations?
options: Arrow functions inherit 'this' lexically from their enclosing scope
Arrow functions bind their own dynamic this
Arrow functions can be used as constructors
2.explanation: Arrow functions do not have their own 'this'; they lexically capture 'this' from the outer context.

2.question: Can an arrow function be used as a constructor with the 'new' keyword?
options: Only if it returns an object
No, calling new on an arrow function throws a TypeError
2.explanation: Arrow functions lack a [[Construct]] internal method and prototype, so 'new' cannot be used with them.
Passing undefined triggers the default parameter value ('Guest').
...nums gathers all arguments into an array [1, 2, 3, 4], which sums to 10.

2.question: What is an IIFE in JavaScript?
options: An Immediately Invoked Function Expression executed as soon as defined
An Interface for Input Form Events
2.explanation: An IIFE (function() { ... })(); runs immediately upon definition.

2.question: What does function hoisting allow you to do in JavaScript?
options: Call a function declaration before its definition in the code
2.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted completely to the top of their scope.

options: Throws TypeError: myFunc is not a function
2.explanation: var myFunc is hoisted as undefined, so attempting to invoke undefined() throws a TypeError.

2.question: What is a pure function?
options: A function that always returns the same output for the same arguments and produces no side effects
2.explanation: Pure functions are deterministic and do not mutate external state or variables.

2.question: What is a higher-order function in JavaScript?
options: A function inside a class constructor
A function with high CPU priority
A function that accepts another function as an argument or returns a function
2.explanation: Higher-order functions (like map, filter, setTimeout) take or return other functions.
Because 'var' is function-scoped, all timeouts reference the same variable 'i' after the loop finishes (i = 3).

2.question: If you replace 'var' with 'let' in the previous loop (for let i = 0; i < 3; i++), what is logged?
2.explanation: 'let' creates a fresh binding for 'i' for each loop iteration, printing 0, 1, 2.

2.question: What does the 'arguments' object in a regular function contain?
options: An array-like object of all arguments passed into the function
2.explanation: The 'arguments' object is an array-like list of all arguments supplied to a non-arrow function.

2.question: What is the difference between Array.prototype.slice() and Array.prototype.splice()?
options: slice mutates the array; splice does not
slice returns a shallow copy of a portion without modifying the original array; splice modifies the original array
2.explanation: slice(start, end) is non-mutating, while splice(start, deleteCount, items) alters the original array.
push adds an element to the end of the array and returns the new length (4).

2.question: Which array method removes the LAST element from an array and returns it?
2.explanation: pop() removes and returns the last element of an array.

2.question: Which array method removes the FIRST element from an array?
2.explanation: shift() removes the first element from index 0 and shifts remaining elements down.

2.question: Which array method adds one or more elements to the BEGINNING of an array?
2.explanation: unshift() inserts elements at the start of an array and returns the new length.

3.explanation: map() transforms each element into a new array: [2, 4, 6].
filter() returns a new array containing all elements that satisfy the predicate: [20, 25].
reduce() accumulates all values: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

3.question: What does Array.prototype.find() return if no matching element is found?
3.explanation: find() returns the first element that satisfies the testing function, or undefined if none match.

3.question: What does Array.prototype.findIndex() return if no matching element is found?
3.explanation: findIndex() returns the index of the first match, or -1 if no element passes the test.

3.question: What will be the output of: [10, 5, 20, 1].sort() without a comparator function?
3.explanation: Default sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units: '1' < '10' < '20' < '5'.

3.question: How do you sort numbers in ascending numeric order in JavaScript?
3.explanation: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b) performs proper ascending numerical sorting.

3.question: What does Array.isArray([1, 2, 3]) return?
3.explanation: Array.isArray() reliably determines whether the passed value is an Array.

3.question: What does [1, 2, 3].includes(2) evaluate to?
3.explanation: includes() checks if an array contains a specified value, returning a boolean (true).

3.question: How can you create a shallow copy of an array 'arr' using the spread operator?
3.explanation: const copy = [...arr]; spreads the elements of arr into a new array.

3.question: How do you extract properties 'name' and 'age' from an object 'user' using ES6 destructuring?
3.explanation: Object destructuring uses curly braces: const { name, age } = user;.

3.question: How do you provide a default value in destructuring if 'role' is undefined?
3.explanation: const { role = 'User' } = user; assigns 'User' if role is undefined.

3.question: What does Object.keys(obj) return?
options: An array of the object's enumerable property names (keys)
An array of the object's enumerable property values
3.explanation: Object.keys(obj) returns an array of a given object's own enumerable property names.

3.question: What does Object.entries(obj) return?
3.explanation: Object.entries(obj) returns an array of the given object's own enumerable string-keyed [key, value] pairs.

3.question: What does Object.freeze(obj) do?
options: Freezes the object, preventing new properties from being added, removed, or existing properties modified
3.explanation: Object.freeze() prevents all modifications to the direct properties of an object.
The object spread operator copies all enumerable properties from 'a' into the new object 'b'.

3.question: What happens when two merged objects share the same property name (e.g. { ...{a: 1}, ...{a: 2} })?
options: The property from the latter object overrides the earlier one ({a: 2})
Both are combined into an array [1, 2]
3.explanation: Properties defined later in the spread order overwrite earlier properties with matching keys.

3.question: What is the difference between dot notation (obj.key) and bracket notation (obj[key])?
options: Dot notation evaluates variables as keys; bracket notation does not
Bracket notation allows dynamic property names and strings with special characters/spaces; dot notation does not
3.explanation: Bracket notation obj[expr] evaluates dynamic expressions and handles keys with hyphens or spaces.

3.question: How do you check if an object 'obj' has an own property 'score'?
3.explanation: Object.hasOwn(obj, 'score') or Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty safely checks for own properties.

3.question: What will be the output of: console.log({} === {});?
3.explanation: In JavaScript, objects and arrays are compared by reference memory location, not by content.

4.explanation: 'ref' and 'obj' reference the exact same memory location, so updating ref.val modifies obj.val.

4.question: How can you make a deep clone of a nested serializable JavaScript object in modern JS without libraries?
4.explanation: structuredClone(obj) is the native browser API for deep-cloning objects and nested structures.

4.question: What do template literals use for string interpolation in ES6?
4.explanation: Template literals use backticks (``) and ${variable} syntax.

4.question: What is the output of: 'Hello World'.includes('World');?
4.explanation: includes() checks for substring presence, returning true.

4.question: What will: 'JavaScript'.slice(0, 4) return?
4.explanation: slice(0, 4) extracts characters from index 0 up to (but not including) index 4: 'Java'.

4.question: What does ' apple '.trim() return?
4.explanation: trim() strips whitespace from both ends of a string.

4.question: What will 'a,b,c'.split(',') return?
4.explanation: split(',') divides a string into an array of substrings based on the specified separator.

4.question: What will ['a', 'b', 'c'].join('-') return?
4.explanation: join('-') concatenates array elements into a single string separated by hyphens.

4.question: What will 'hello'.charAt(1) return?
4.explanation: Strings are 0-indexed; index 1 is 'e'.

4.question: What does 'hello'.startsWith('he') return?
4.explanation: startsWith('he') returns true because 'hello' begins with 'he'.

4.question: What will: 'foo'.repeat(3) return?
4.explanation: repeat(3) creates and returns a new string containing the specified number of copies.

4.question: What is the output of: '123'.padStart(5, '0')?
4.explanation: padStart(5, '0') pads the start of the string with '0' until reaching length 5.

4.question: What is the return type of document.querySelector('.btn')?
options: An array of all matching elements
The first matching Element node in the document, or null
4.explanation: querySelector returns the first matching element, or null if none is found.

4.question: What is the return type of document.querySelectorAll('p')?
options: A static NodeList of all matching elements
4.explanation: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList of all elements matching the CSS selector.

4.question: What is the difference between 'textContent' and 'innerHTML'?
options: They are identical in all aspects
innerHTML is faster and safer against XSS
textContent returns plain text without parsing HTML tags; innerHTML parses and renders HTML tags
textContent renders HTML markup; innerHTML treats everything as plain text
4.explanation: textContent sets or gets raw text safely, while innerHTML parses HTML strings into DOM nodes.

4.question: Which method is used to add a new CSS class 'active' to an element's classList?
4.explanation: element.classList.add('active') adds the class without affecting other existing classes.

4.question: Which method toggles a class on an element, adding it if missing and removing it if present?
4.explanation: element.classList.toggle('dark') adds or removes the class based on its current existence.

4.question: Which method creates a new HTML element dynamically in JavaScript?
4.explanation: document.createElement(tagName) creates a new Element node in memory.

4.question: Which method inserts a newly created node at the end of a parent element's children list?
4.explanation: appendChild() or append() attaches a node as the last child of a parent.

4.question: Which method removes an element from the DOM directly in modern browsers?
4.explanation: element.remove() removes the element from its parent DOM tree.

5.question: What does event.preventDefault() do in an event handler?
options: Prevents the default browser action associated with the event (e.g. form submission reloading the page)
Stops the event from bubbling up the DOM tree
5.explanation: event.preventDefault() stops the browser's default behavior, such as preventing a form from submitting/refreshing.

5.question: What does event.stopPropagation() do in JavaScript event handling?
options: Stops the event from bubbling up or capturing down through ancestor elements
5.explanation: event.stopPropagation() prevents further propagation of the current event in the capturing and bubbling phases.

5.question: What is Event Delegation in JavaScript?
options: A design pattern for creating custom events
Delegating event handling to a Web Worker
Attaching a single event listener to a common parent element to handle events on dynamic children via bubbling
Attaching separate event listeners to every single child element
5.explanation: Event delegation uses event bubbling to manage handlers on a parent element for multiple or dynamically added children.

5.question: Which parameter in element.addEventListener('click', fn, useCapture) enables the capturing phase?
5.explanation: Passing true as the third argument invokes the listener during the capturing phase rather than the default bubbling phase.

5.question: Which event fires when the value of an <input> element is changed by user keystrokes in real time?
5.explanation: The 'input' event fires synchronously every time the value of an input or textarea changes.

5.question: What is the difference between the 'input' event and the 'change' event on text inputs?
options: 'input' fires on blur; 'change' fires on every keystroke
'input' fires immediately on every keystroke; 'change' fires only after the input loses focus (blur) and value was modified
5.explanation: 'input' fires immediately with each character change; 'change' triggers when committed/blurred.

5.question: What does JSON.stringify(data) do?
options: Parses a JSON string into a JavaScript object
Converts a JavaScript object/value into a standard JSON string
5.explanation: JSON.stringify() serializes a JavaScript object into a JSON formatted string.

5.question: What does JSON.parse(text) do?
options: Parses a JSON string and constructs the JavaScript value or object described
Converts an object to a string
5.explanation: JSON.parse() deserializes a JSON string into a JavaScript object.

5.question: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
options: sessionStorage is shared across all windows
localStorage persists data across browser sessions/restarts; sessionStorage data is cleared when the browser tab is closed
5.explanation: localStorage has no expiration time; sessionStorage is scoped to the tab lifetime.
